blocks.prompt: How a Fish Breathes Water
blocks.text: You breathe air. A fish cannot. So a fish does something clever with its mouth. Watch a fish in a tank. Its mouth opens and closes all day long. It is not eating. It is breathing. The fish takes a gulp of water. It pushes the water back over its gills. The gills are red and feathery, and they sit behind a flap on each side of the head. There is a little bit of air hiding in the water. The gills grab it. Then the used water slips out the flap, and the fish gulps again.

3.title: How a Fish Breathes Water
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

blocks.prompt: The Trick of Breathing Water
blocks.text: Air is easy to breathe. It is about one fifth oxygen, and it is light, so your chest barely works to move it. Water is a much harder place to live. A mouthful of water holds around thirty times less oxygen than a mouthful of air, and water is heavy. A fish has to move a lot of it to get a little. So a fish never stops working. It gulps water in through its mouth and pushes it out over its gills. Gills look like red feathers, stacked in rows behind a bony flap. Each feather is covered in even smaller folds, so the gill has a huge surface pressed against the water. Oxygen slips out of the water and into the fish's blood. The tired water washes away out the flap. A fish is doing this every second of its life. It is the reason a fish out of water dies so fast. On land the gill feathers stick together in a wet clump. There is plenty of oxygen all around, and the fish has no way left to reach it.

answers: water holds about thirty times less oxygen than air, and it is heavy to move

4.title: How a Fish Breathes Water
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The lateral line feels water move

blocks.prompt: The Line Down a Fish's Side
blocks.text: Look closely at a fish and you will find a faint line running from its gill flap to its tail. It is easy to mistake for a scratch. It is a sense organ, and you do not have anything like it. The line is a row of tiny pores in the skin. Under each pore sits a bundle of hair cells in jelly. When water moves, the jelly bends, and the fish feels it. That is the whole trick: a fish feels water the way you feel a breeze on your arm, except it can feel a shape in the water it has not seen. A hand reaching into a tank pushes a small wall of water ahead of it, and the fish knows before it looks. This is how a school of hundreds turns as one body without crashing. It is how a blind cave fish, with no eyes at all, maps a cave wall it cannot see. A fish carries another quiet invention inside it. Most bony fish have a swim bladder, a balloon of gas tucked under the spine. Add gas and the fish floats up. Take gas out and it sinks. Once the bladder is set, the fish can hang motionless in the water without a single flick of a fin. Sharks were never given one. A shark has a huge oily liver instead, and many kinds must keep swimming or slowly settle to the bottom.

5.title: How a Fish Breathes Water
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Water holds about 30x less oxygen than air
Water is about 800x denser than air
Countercurrent: blood and water run opposite ways
Gills can pull out up to 80% of the oxygen
Human lungs manage about 25%
Gill surface can exceed the whole fish's skin

blocks.prompt: Thirty Times Less Air
blocks.text: Breathing air is close to free. Air is about twenty one percent oxygen, it weighs almost nothing, and your lungs take what they need with a movement so small you forget you are doing it. Water is a far meaner deal. A liter of seawater carries roughly thirty times less oxygen than a liter of air, and water is around eight hundred times denser. A fish must therefore shift a heavy, stingy fluid across its body, all day, forever, and it may spend a tenth of its energy simply on the act of breathing. Given that bill, evolution built the fish a better lung than yours. Water enters the mouth and is driven out across four gill arches on each side. Each arch carries rows of filaments, and each filament is stacked with thousands of thin plates called lamellae. Fold upon fold, the surface adds up to something enormous, often larger than the outside of the entire fish. Blood runs through those plates under a skin only a cell or two thick. The clever part is the direction. Inside each lamella, blood flows one way and water flows the other. They pass each other head on. This is called countercurrent exchange, and it means that blood which has already collected plenty of oxygen still meets water that is fresher and richer than itself. All the way along, the gradient holds. Oxygen keeps crossing, from the first plate to the last. Compare that to your own chest. Your lungs are a dead end. Air goes in, mixes with stale air already sitting there, and comes back out the way it came, and you strip out around a quarter of the oxygen you inhaled. A fish, working in water that barely has any, pulls out as much as eighty percent. So the next time you watch a goldfish work its mouth, notice what you are looking at. It is not idle. It is running one of the most efficient gas exchangers on the planet, and it cannot stop for a second.

6.title: How a Fish Breathes Water
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Ray fins and lobe fins split about 420 million years ago
Lungfish are our closest living relatives in the water
'Fish' is paraphyletic, not a true branch
The swim bladder and your lungs are the same old organ
'Reptile' had the same flaw until birds were added
About 34,000 named species and counting

blocks.prompt: There Is No Such Thing as a Fish
blocks.text: Start with a fact that sounds like a trick and is not. A lungfish is more closely related to you than it is to a salmon. That claim is not about size or cleverness or where an animal lives. It is about ancestry, and ancestry is the only family tree biology recognizes. Roughly four hundred and twenty million years ago, the bony vertebrates split into two great limbs. One limb, the ray fins, went on to produce the salmon, the goldfish, the tuna, and very nearly every fish you could name. The other limb, the lobe fins, produced coelacanths, lungfish, and every animal that has ever walked on land, including you. Within that second limb, the lungfish are our nearest living relatives left in the water. So a lungfish and a person share a more recent ancestor than a lungfish and a salmon do. The tree says so, and the tree is not taking votes. Now count what that means. Any group called 'fish' that contains both the salmon and the lungfish, but leaves you out, is not a real group. It is a bag with a hole in the bottom. Biologists have a word for this: paraphyletic, a category made by taking a genuine branch of the tree and quietly deleting some of the descendants you would rather not talk about. 'Fish' is such a category. So was 'reptile' until birds were let in. The honest version is that a fish is not a kind of animal. It is a job description. It means: a vertebrate that lives in water, breathes with gills, and swims with fins. Hagfish, sharks, sturgeon, seahorses, and lungfish all do that job, and they are separated from one another by hundreds of millions of years. Some have skeletons of bone and some of cartilage. Some have jaws and some have never had them. Calling them all fish tells you what they do for a living. It tells you almost nothing about who they are. The evidence for the tree is hiding inside the animals themselves. Consider the swim bladder, the gas filled sac that lets a bony fish hang weightless in the water. It looks like a marvel of underwater engineering, so it is strange to learn that it is a modified lung. Early bony fishes in warm, oxygen poor shallows gulped air into a pouch off the gut, and that pouch is the same organ that became a lung in one lineage and a buoyancy tank in another. Your chest and a goldfish's swim bladder are the same idea, running in different directions for four hundred million years. None of this means the word should be thrown away. Ecology needs it. If you study who eats whom in a reef, 'fish' is a useful and honest word, because the reef cares what an animal does, not who its ancestors were. The lesson is smaller and sharper than that. It is that some of our oldest, most obvious categories were drawn by eye, from the outside, by people standing on a shore. When the evidence arrived, the categories did not survive contact with it. That happens more often than we like to admit, and the word 'fish' is simply the case where it is easiest to see.
